questions.question: Let a tangent be drawn to the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{27}+y^2=1$ at $(3\sqrt3\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ where $\theta\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$. Then the value of $\theta$ such that the sum of intercepts on axes made by this tangent is minimum is equal to -
questions.key_idea: The tangent has intercepts $3\sqrt3\sec\theta$ and $\csc\theta$; minimise their sum with $f'(\theta)=0$.
solution: $f'<0$ just before $\frac\pi6$ and $f'>0$ just after it (the $\sin^3\theta$ term grows, the $\cos^3\theta$ term shrinks), so this is a minimum; $f\left(\frac\pi6\right)=6+2=8$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Hölder's inequality bounds $\frac{a}{\cos\theta}+\frac{b}{\sin\theta}$ below with no derivative.

useful_results: Tangent to $\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ at $(a\cos\theta,b\sin\theta)$ is $\frac{x\cos\theta}{a}+\frac{y\sin\theta}{b}=1$, with intercepts $a\sec\theta$ and $b\csc\theta$.
$\min\left(a\sec\theta+b\csc\theta\right)=\left(a^{2/3}+b^{2/3}\right)^{3/2}$ at $\tan\theta=\left(\frac ba\right)^{1/3}$ (here $a=3\sqrt3,b=1$ gives $8$ at $\theta=\frac\pi6$).
The shortest tangent segment between the axes has length $a+b$, and the least area of the triangle cut off is $ab$.

questions.question: The position of a moving car at time $t$ is given by $f(t)=at^2+bt+c$, $t>0$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are real numbers greater than $1$. Then the average speed of the car over the time interval $[t_1,t_2]$ is attained at the point :
questions.key_idea: Lagrange's mean value theorem: the average rate $\frac{f(t_2)-f(t_1)}{t_2-t_1}$ equals $f'(t)$ at some interior $t$.
solution: $f$ is a polynomial, hence continuous on $[t_1,t_2]$ and differentiable on $(t_1,t_2)$, so Lagrange's mean value theorem applies.
Hence $2at=a(t_1+t_2)$, i.e. $t=\frac{t_1+t_2}{2}$ (as $a>1$, so $a\ne0$). Since $f'(t)=2at+b>0$ the speed equals the velocity, so this is where the average speed is attained.

alternate_solutions.idea: Centre the time at the midpoint $m=\frac{t_1+t_2}2$: the even part of a quadratic cancels in the chord slope.
solution: Put $t=m+u$ with $m=\frac{t_1+t_2}2$ and $h=\frac{t_2-t_1}2$, so the interval is $u\in[-h,h]$.
Chord slope $=\frac{f(m+h)-f(m-h)}{2h}$. The terms $au^2$ and the constant are even in $u$, so they cancel; only $(2am+b)(2h)$ survives.
So $V_{avg}=2am+b$, which is exactly $f'(m)$ because $f'(m+u)=2au+(2am+b)$ at $u=0$.
Hence the average speed is attained at $t=m=\frac{t_1+t_2}{2}$.

useful_results: For every quadratic $\alpha t^2+\beta t+\gamma$ the mean-value point of $[t_1,t_2]$ is the midpoint $\frac{t_1+t_2}2$ (the tangent at the midpoint is parallel to the chord - Archimedes' property of the parabola).
The mean-value point does not depend on $a$, $b$, $c$; for a cubic it is not the midpoint (for $t^3$ on $[t_1,t_2]$: $\xi^2=m^2+\frac{h^2}{3}$).
If $f'$ is linear, the average of $f'$ over $[t_1,t_2]$ equals $\frac{f'(t_1)+f'(t_2)}2=f'(\text{midpoint})$.

questions.question: If $\left(a+\sqrt2b\cos x\right)\left(a-\sqrt2b\cos y\right)=a^2-b^2$, where $a>b>0$, then $\frac{dx}{dy}$ at $\left(\frac\pi4,\frac\pi4\right)$ is :
questions.key_idea: Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a function of $x$, then invert $\frac{dy}{dx}$.
solution: The relation is $\left(a+\sqrt2b\cos x\right)\left(a-\sqrt2b\cos y\right)=a^2-b^2$. Differentiate with respect to $x$ (product rule).

alternate_solutions.idea: Take logarithms: for a product $u(x)v(y)=\text{const}$, $\frac{u'}{u}dx+\frac{v'}{v}dy=0$ gives $\frac{dx}{dy}$ directly.
solution: The point lies on the curve: $(a+b)(a-b)=a^2-b^2$, and both factors are positive, so take $\ln$: $\ln\left(a+\sqrt2b\cos x\right)+\ln\left(a-\sqrt2b\cos y\right)=\ln(a^2-b^2)$.
Differentiate in differentials: $\frac{-\sqrt2b\sin x}{a+\sqrt2b\cos x}dx+\frac{\sqrt2b\sin y}{a-\sqrt2b\cos y}dy=0$.
So $\frac{b}{a+b}dx=\frac{b}{a-b}dy$ and $\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{a+b}{a-b}$ directly - no inversion needed.

useful_results: For $F(x,y)=0$: $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{F_x}{F_y}$ and $\frac{dx}{dy}=-\frac{F_y}{F_x}$, so $\frac{dx}{dy}$ can be found in one step by differentiating with respect to $y$.
For a product $u(x)v(y)=k$ use logarithmic differentiation: $\frac{dx}{dy}=-\frac{v'(y)/v(y)}{u'(x)/u(x)}$.
Always confirm the given point lies on the curve; here $(a+b)(a-b)=a^2-b^2$ does.

questions.question: If $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin^{-1}x-\tan^{-1}x}{3x^3}$ is equal to $L$, then the value of $(6L+1)$ is :
questions.key_idea: The limit is of $\frac00$ form; one application of L'Hôpital's rule leaves a quotient that rationalises to $\frac16$.
solution: As $x\to0$, $\sin^{-1}x-\tan^{-1}x\to0$ and $3x^3\to0$: the form is $\frac00$, so apply L'Hôpital's rule.
Multiply numerator and denominator by $1+x^2+\sqrt{1-x^2}$: the numerator becomes $(1+x^2)^2-(1-x^2)=x^4+3x^2$.
$L=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{x^4+3x^2}{\sqrt{1-x^2}\,(1+x^2)\,9x^2\left(1+x^2+\sqrt{1-x^2}\right)}$; the factors other than $9x^2$ tend to $1\cdot1\cdot2=2$ in the denominator.

alternate_solutions.idea: Maclaurin series: $\sin^{-1}x=x+\frac{x^3}6+\dots$ and $\tan^{-1}x=x-\frac{x^3}3+\dots$ expose the $x^3$ coefficient at once.

useful_results: Standard expansions: $\sin^{-1}x=x+\frac{x^3}6+\dots$, $\tan^{-1}x=x-\frac{x^3}3+\dots$, $\sin x=x-\frac{x^3}6+\dots$, $\tan x=x+\frac{x^3}3+\dots$.
Hence $\sin^{-1}x-\tan^{-1}x\sim\frac{x^3}2$, $\tan x-\sin x\sim\frac{x^3}2$, $\sin^{-1}x-x\sim\frac{x^3}6$ and $x-\tan^{-1}x\sim\frac{x^3}3$ as $x\to0$.
When two functions agree to first order, their difference is governed by the $x^3$ coefficients - L'Hôpital twice or a series both work, but the series is faster.

questions.question: Let $y=f(x)=\sin^3\left(\frac\pi3\left(\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3\sqrt2}\left(-4x^3+5x^2+1\right)^{3/2}\right)\right)\right)$. Then, at $x=1$,
questions.key_idea: Split into layers $g\to v\to u\to y$, differentiate layer by layer, and evaluate each layer at $x=1$ where the angles are standard.
solution: Values of the factors at $x=1$: $\sin^2u=\frac14$, $\cos u=\frac{\sqrt3}2$, $\sin v=\frac{\sqrt3}2$, $\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{\pi}{3\sqrt2}\cdot\frac32\cdot\sqrt2\cdot(-2)=-\pi$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $\sin^3u=\frac{3\sin u-\sin3u}{4}$; at $u=-\frac\pi6$ the term $\cos3u$ vanishes, so $y'$ is a single product.

useful_results: $\sin^3u=\frac{3\sin u-\sin3u}4$ and $\cos^3u=\frac{3\cos u+\cos3u}4$ turn a power into a sum and often make a derivative evaluate at a special angle.

For a tower of functions, first compute the inner values at the given point (here $g=2$, $v=\frac{2\pi}3$, $u=-\frac\pi6$) - the designed values are standard angles; only then multiply the local derivatives.
$\frac{d}{dx}g^{3/2}=\frac32\sqrt g\,g'$. When the options are linear relations between $y$ and $y'$, compute $y$ and $y'$ separately and substitute.

questions.question: Consider the function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(x)=\begin{cases}\left(2\sin\left(\frac1x\right)\right)|x|, & x\ne0\\ 0, & x=0\end{cases}$. Then $f$ is:
questions.key_idea: Near $0$ the derivative $2\sin\frac1x-\frac2x\cos\frac1x$ keeps changing sign, so $f$ cannot be monotonic on either side.
solution: At $x=\frac1{2n\pi}$ ($n\ge1$): $\sin\frac1x=0$, $\cos\frac1x=1$, so $f'(x)=-4n\pi<0$; the same value occurs at $x=-\frac1{2n\pi}$ (here $f'$ is even because $f$ is odd).
At $x=\frac1{(2n+1)\pi}$: $\sin\frac1x=0$, $\cos\frac1x=-1$, so $f'(x)=2(2n+1)\pi>0$; again the same value at $x=-\frac1{(2n+1)\pi}$.
So $f'$ takes both signs in every interval $(0,\delta)$ and $(-\delta,0)$: $f'(x)$ is an oscillating function and $f$ is not monotonic on $(0,\infty)$ nor on $(-\infty,0)$.
Hence (A) and (B) fail (monotonic on one side only is false) and (D) fails too: the answer is (C).
questions.correction_note: The question prints f(x) = (2 sin(1/x))|x|, but the PDF's solution works with f(x) = (2 - sin(1/x))x for x>0 and -(2 - sin(1/x))x for x<0, i.e. a different function (the intended one is probably (2 - sin(1/x))|x|; the printed question looks like a misprint of it). I solved the printed function. Both functions are non-monotonic on each side (for 2 - sin(1/x): f' = 2 - sin(1/x) + cos(1/x)/x is +ve at x=1/(2n pi) and -ve at x=1/((2n+1)pi) for n>=1), so the key (C) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Compare values: $f$ vanishes at $\frac1{n\pi}$ but is positive and negative in between, so it goes up and down - no derivative needed.
solution: Take also $z_k=\frac{1}{k\pi}$ where $f(z_k)=0$. The points interlace: $\frac2{7\pi}<\frac1{3\pi}<\frac2{5\pi}<\frac1{2\pi}$.
Moving to the right the values go $-,0,+,0$: increasing from $\frac2{7\pi}$ to $\frac2{5\pi}$, then decreasing to $\frac1{2\pi}$. So $f$ is not monotonic on $(0,\infty)$.

$f$ is odd ($f(-x)=2|x|\sin\left(-\frac1x\right)=-f(x)$), and an odd function is increasing on $(0,\infty)$ iff it is increasing on $(-\infty,0)$ (same for decreasing). So $f$ is not monotonic on $(-\infty,0)$ either: (C).

useful_results: $x\sin\frac1x$ (with value $0$ at $0$) is continuous at $0$ but is not monotone in any neighbourhood of $0$; its zeros $\frac1{n\pi}$ and extrema near $\frac2{(2k+1)\pi}$ alternate.

If $f$ is odd, then monotonicity on $(0,\infty)$ and on $(-\infty,0)$ are equivalent (same direction); for an even function the directions are opposite. So 'monotonic on exactly one side' is impossible for odd or even $f$.
Monotonic $\Rightarrow$ $f'$ of constant sign; an oscillating derivative with unbounded swings (here $\frac{2}{x}\cos\frac1x$) rules out monotonicity.

concepts: Principal values of inverse trigonometric functions
questions.question: If $2y=\left(\cot^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt3\cos x+\sin x}{\cos x-\sqrt3\sin x}\right)\right)^2$, $x\in\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$ then $\frac{dy}{dx}$ is equal to
questions.key_idea: Divide by $2$ to get $\frac{\cos(\frac\pi6-x)}{\sin(\frac\pi6-x)}=\cot\left(\frac\pi6-x\right)$, then reduce into the principal range $(0,\pi)$ of $\cot^{-1}$.
solution: Divide numerator and denominator by $2$: $\frac{\frac{\sqrt3}2\cos x+\frac12\sin x}{\frac12\cos x-\frac{\sqrt3}2\sin x}=\frac{\cos\left(\frac\pi6-x\right)}{\sin\left(\frac\pi6-x\right)}$.

Only one of the given options can match: $x-\frac\pi6$, which is option (B) (for $x\in\left(0,\frac\pi6\right)$; on $\left(\frac\pi6,\frac\pi2\right)$ the derivative is $x-\frac{7\pi}6$, which is not among the options).
questions.correction_note: Two things. (1) The PDF's second line writes the denominator as 1/2 cos x + (sqrt3/2) sin x, which is a sign slip; the question has cos x - sqrt3 sin x, i.e. 1/2 cos x - (sqrt3/2) sin x = sin(pi/6 - x). The PDF's next line (sin(pi/6 - x)) is right, so only the displayed middle step is fixed. (2) The PDF does not say that the key (B) holds only for x in (0, pi/6); on (pi/6, pi/2) the derivative is x - 7pi/6. This is stated in the last bullet. (Also 2y jumps at x = pi/6 where the argument is undefined.)

alternate_solutions.idea: Divide by $\cos x$: the argument is $\tan\left(\frac\pi3+x\right)$, so $\cot^{-1}=\frac\pi2-\tan^{-1}(\cdot)$ and branches follow from $\tan^{-1}\tan\theta$.
solution: Divide the numerator and denominator by $\cos x$: $\frac{\sqrt3+\tan x}{1-\sqrt3\tan x}=\tan\left(\frac\pi3+x\right)$.
Differentiating gives $\frac{dy}{dx}=x-\frac\pi6$ on $\left(0,\frac\pi6\right)$ and $x-\frac{7\pi}6$ on $\left(\frac\pi6,\frac\pi2\right)$ - the same as before.

useful_results: $\cot^{-1}(\cot t)=t-k\pi$ where $k$ is the integer with $t-k\pi\in(0,\pi)$; $\tan^{-1}(\tan t)=t-k\pi$ with $t-k\pi\in\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$. Always locate the angle in the principal range before simplifying.
$a\cos x+b\sin x=R\cos(x-\alpha)$ and $\frac{\sqrt3\cos x+\sin x}{\cos x-\sqrt3\sin x}=\cot\left(\frac\pi6-x\right)=\tan\left(\frac\pi3+x\right)$ - spot the $\frac\pi6$ and $\frac\pi3$ angles.
A branch change makes the function jump (here at $x=\frac\pi6$): the derivative formula can differ on each side. Check which interval the option corresponds to.

questions.question: If $f(x)$ is a non-zero polynomial of degree four, having local extreme points at $x=-1,0,1$; then the set $S=\{x\in\mathbb{R}:f(x)=f(0)\}$ contains exactly :
options: Two irrational and one rational number
Two irrational and two rational numbers
questions.answer: (C) Two irrational and one rational number
questions.key_idea: A quartic with critical points $-1,0,1$ has $f'(x)=A(x+1)x(x-1)$, so $f(x)-f(0)=A\left(\frac{x^4}4-\frac{x^2}2\right)$.
solution: $f$ has degree $4$, so $f'$ has degree $3$; its roots are the local extreme points $-1,0,1$, so $f'(x)=A(x+1)\,x\,(x-1)$ with $A\ne0$.
$S=\{0,-\sqrt2,\sqrt2\}$: one rational number ($0$) and two irrational numbers ($\pm\sqrt2$), so (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Symmetry: $f'$ is odd, so $f$ is even; $f(x)-f(0)$ is then even with a double root at $0$ and has the form $x^2(\alpha x^2+\beta)$.
solution: Critical points $-1,0,1$ are symmetric and $f'$ is a cubic with these three roots, so $f'(x)=A(x^3-x)$ is an odd function.
An even-degree polynomial whose derivative is odd is even: $f(x)=\alpha x^4+\beta x^2+C$ (no odd powers).
Then $f(x)-f(0)=\alpha x^4+\beta x^2=x^2\left(\alpha x^2+\beta\right)$, with $\alpha\ne0$; $x=0$ is a root (double).
$f'(x)=4\alpha x^3+2\beta x=A(x^3-x)$ gives $\beta=-2\alpha$ (compare the ratio of coefficients: $\frac{2\beta}{4\alpha}=-1$).
So $f(x)-f(0)=\alpha x^2\left(x^2-2\right)$, with roots $0,\pm\sqrt2$: one rational and two irrational numbers (C).

useful_results: A polynomial of degree $n$ with $n-1$ distinct critical points has $f'(x)=A\prod(x-c_i)$; its derivative is determined up to the constant $A$.
If $f'$ is odd then $f$ is even (and if $f'$ is even then $f=\text{odd}+C$). Then $f(x)=f(0)$ is a polynomial equation in $x^2$.
Each root of $f(x)=f(0)$ that is also a critical point (here $x=0$) is a repeated root; the set $S$ lists it once.

questions.question: The function $f(x)=\frac{4x^3-3x^2}{6}-2\sin x+(2x-1)\cos x$ :
questions.key_idea: The terms $\mp2\cos x$ cancel in $f'$, leaving $f'(x)=(2x-1)(x-\sin x)$, and $x-\sin x\ge0$ for $x\ge0$.
solution: $\frac{d}{dx}\left[-2\sin x+(2x-1)\cos x\right]=-2\cos x+2\cos x-(2x-1)\sin x=-(2x-1)\sin x$.
For $x\ge0$ we have $x\ge\sin x$ (equality only at $x=0$), so $x-\sin x\ge0$; for $x\ge\frac12$ also $2x-1\ge0$.
Hence $f'(x)\ge0$ for $x\in\left[\frac12,\infty\right)$ ($=0$ only at $x=\frac12$): $f(x)$ is increasing for $x\in\left[\frac12,\infty\right)$.

Option (A) is false ($f'\ge0$ there). For $0<x<\frac12$, $2x-1<0$ and $x-\sin x>0$, so $f'<0$ there: $f$ is not increasing on $\left(-\infty,\frac12\right]$ (C false). For $x<0$, $f'>0$, so $f$ is not decreasing on $\left(-\infty,\frac12\right]$ (B false). Answer (D).
useful_results: $x>\sin x$ for $x>0$ and $x<\sin x$ for $x<0$, so $x-\sin x$ has the sign of $x$ and vanishes only at $0$.

$\frac{d}{dx}\left[(\alpha x+\beta)\cos x-\alpha\sin x\right]=-(\alpha x+\beta)\sin x$: such terms cancel the $\cos x$ part in $f'$ (integration-by-parts pattern); in this question $\alpha=2,\beta=-1$.
If $f'=(\text{linear})\times(\text{factor of fixed sign on a half-line})$, the sign table is read from the linear factor alone; check the other half-lines for the options that say 'decreasing'.

concepts: Bounds on a function and its derivative from derivative inequalities
questions.question: Let $f$ be a twice differentiable function on $(1,6)$. If $f(2)=8$, $f'(2)=5$, $f'(x)\ge1$ and $f''(x)\ge4$, for all $x\in(1,6)$, then :
questions.key_idea: Integrate $f'\ge1$ and $f''\ge4$ over $[2,5]$ to bound $f(5)$ and $f'(5)$ from below.
solution: Options (B) and (C) contradict (I) and (II) (they would need $f(5)+f'(5)\le26$, $f(5)\le10$); (D) fails as $f'(5)+f''(5)\ge17+4=21>20$. Hence (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Taylor's theorem with Lagrange remainder: $f''\ge4$ forces $f$ above the parabola $8+5(x-2)+2(x-2)^2$.
solution: Taylor with remainder about $2$: $f(5)=f(2)+f'(2)(3)+\frac{f''(\xi)}{2}(3)^2$ for some $\xi\in(2,5)$.
For the derivative, apply the mean value theorem to $f'$ on $[2,5]$: $f'(5)-f'(2)=3f''(\eta)\ge12$, so $f'(5)\ge17$.
Hence $f(5)+f'(5)\ge41+17=58\ge28$, so option (A) holds (with room to spare).
The sharper bounds also reject the others at once: $f(5)\ge41>10$ kills (C) and (B), and $f'(5)+f''(5)\ge17+4=21>20$ kills (D).

useful_results: If $f''\ge k$ on $[a,b]$ then $f'(b)\ge f'(a)+k(b-a)$ and $f(b)\ge f(a)+f'(a)(b-a)+\frac k2(b-a)^2$ (the graph lies above the parabola with second derivative $k$).
Inequalities between functions may be integrated over an interval: $g\ge h\Rightarrow\int g\ge\int h$. Do it twice for a bound on $f''$.
The first-order bound ($f(5)\ge11$) is weaker than the second-order one ($f(5)\ge41$), but both are valid and either is enough here.

questions.question: Let $f(x)=\left(\sin(\tan^{-1}x)+\sin(\cot^{-1}x)\right)^2-1$, $|x|>1$. If $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac12\frac{d}{dx}\left(\sin^{-1}(f(x))\right)$ and $y(\sqrt3)=\frac\pi6$, then $y(-\sqrt3)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $f(x)=\sin(2\tan^{-1}x)$, and $\sin^{-1}\sin\theta$ must be reduced to $[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2]$ separately for $x>1$ and $x<-1$.
solution: Both expressions have the same derivative $-\frac2{1+x^2}$, so $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac12\cdot\left(-\frac{2}{1+x^2}\right)=-\frac1{1+x^2}$, i.e. $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac12\frac{d}{dx}\left(\pi-2\tan^{-1}x\right)$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes sin^-1 f(x) = pi - 2 tan^-1 x 'since x = sqrt3' and then uses the same formula for x = -sqrt3. For x < -1 the correct reduction is sin^-1 f(x) = -pi - 2 tan^-1 x (the PDF's formula is valid only for x > 1). The derivative is the same on both sides (-2/(1+x^2)), so the working still leads to y = -tan^-1 x + c, but the answer 5pi/6 depends on taking ONE constant c for both pieces of the disconnected domain |x|>1 (the question gives y at only one point). Strictly the data do not fix y(-sqrt3); the key (A) is the intended answer under the single-constant reading.

alternate_solutions.idea: Differentiate directly: $f(x)=\frac{2x}{1+x^2}$ and $\sqrt{1-f^2}=\frac{x^2-1}{1+x^2}$ for $|x|>1$, so the branch question never arises.

useful_results: $\tan^{-1}x+\cot^{-1}x=\frac\pi2$ for all real $x$ (principal values $\cot^{-1}x\in(0,\pi)$), so $\sin(\tan^{-1}x)+\sin(\cot^{-1}x)$ becomes $\sin\theta+\cos\theta$.
$\sin^{-1}\frac{2x}{1+x^2}=2\tan^{-1}x$ for $|x|\le1$; $=\pi-2\tan^{-1}x$ for $x\ge1$; $=-\pi-2\tan^{-1}x$ for $x\le-1$ (e.g. at $x=2$ both sides give $0.9273$).
On a disconnected domain (like $|x|>1$) an antiderivative may carry different constants on each piece: $y(\sqrt3)$ alone need not fix $y(-\sqrt3)$ unless a single formula is intended.

concepts: Maxima and minima of the slope of a curve
questions.question: The maximum slope of the curve $y=\frac12x^4-5x^3+18x^2-19x$ occurs at the point :
questions.key_idea: The slope is $m=y'$; its maximum is found from $\frac{dm}{dx}=y''=0$ and the sign change of $y''$.
solution: To find the maximum of $m$ differentiate: $\frac{dm}{dx}=6x^2-30x+36=6(x-2)(x-3)=0\Rightarrow x=2$ or $x=3$.
So $x=2$ is a point of (local) maximum of the slope and $x=3$ is a point of minimum.
The point is $(2,2)$, option (C). (The slope there is $m(2)=16-60+72-19=9$.)

alternate_solutions.idea: Shift to the inflection centre $t=x-\frac52$: the slope becomes $2t^3-\frac32t+\text{const}$, whose local maximum is at $t=-\frac12$.
solution: $m=2t^3-\frac32t+\frac{17}2$ is a cubic with positive leading coefficient and turning points at $t=\pm\frac12$; the left one, $t=-\frac12$ (that is $x=2$), is the local maximum: $m=2\left(-\frac18\right)+\frac34+\frac{17}2=9$.
Check against the other candidates: $m(3)=8<9$ and $m(0)=-19$; $(2,9)$ is not on the curve because $y(2)=2$.
Hence the maximum slope occurs at $x=2$, i.e. at $(2,2)$ (option C).

useful_results: The slope of a curve is largest/smallest where $y''=0$ and $y''$ changes sign: extrema of the slope are inflection points of the curve.
For a quartic with positive leading coefficient the slope $y'$ is a cubic: unbounded in both directions, so 'maximum slope' means the local maximum (at the smaller root of $y''=0$ here, $x=2$).
Give the point, not just $x$: always substitute back into $y$ (an option like $(2,9)$ may not even lie on the curve).

concepts: Optimisation: maximum area of an inscribed triangle
questions.question: The triangle of maximum area that can be inscribed in a given circle of radius 'r' is :
options: A right angle triangle having two of its sides of length $2r$ and $r$.
An equilateral triangle having each of its side of length $\sqrt3\,r$.
An isosceles triangle with base equal to $2r$.
questions.answer: (C) An equilateral triangle having each side of length $\sqrt3\,r$
questions.key_idea: With circumradius $r$: area $\Delta=\frac{abc}{4r}$, and AM-GM with $a+b+c\le3\sqrt3\,r$ bounds it by equality at $a=b=c$.
solution: For a triangle $ABC$ inscribed in a circle of radius $r$, the area is $\Delta=\frac{abc}{4r}$.
$\frac{a}{2r}=\sin A$ etc., so $\frac{a+b+c}{2r}=\sin A+\sin B+\sin C$.

Since $\sin$ is concave on $(0,\pi)$ (centroid of the points $(A,\sin A)$, $(B,\sin B)$, $(C,\sin C)$ lies below the curve): $\frac{\sin A+\sin B+\sin C}{3}\le\sin\left(\frac{A+B+C}{3}\right)=\sin\frac\pi3$.
So $\sin A+\sin B+\sin C\le\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}$, i.e. $\frac{a+b+c}{2r}\le\frac{3\sqrt3}2$ and $\frac{a+b+c}{3}\le\sqrt3\,r$.
So the triangle is equilateral, with side $a=\sqrt3\,r$ (option C). (Option A is false: the height of this triangle is $\frac{3r}2$, not $\frac{2r}3$.)

alternate_solutions.idea: Smoothing: for a fixed side the area is greatest when the third vertex is on the perpendicular bisector, so the maximum triangle has equal sides.
solution: For a fixed chord $BC$, the area $\frac12\cdot BC\cdot(\text{height of }A)$ is greatest when $A$ is farthest from $BC$, i.e. at the midpoint of the major arc: $AB=AC$.
The maximum-area triangle (it exists, as the area is continuous on a compact set of positions) must be optimal for each of its three sides in this way, so $AB=AC$, $BA=BC$ and $CA=CB$.
Hence $a=b=c$: the triangle is equilateral, with $A=B=C=\frac\pi3$ and side $a=2r\sin\frac\pi3=\sqrt3\,r$.

Area $=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}a^2=\frac{\sqrt3}4\cdot3r^2=\frac{3\sqrt3}4r^2$, which beats the others: the isosceles triangle with base $2r$ has area $r^2$, and the right triangle with sides $r$ and $\sqrt3r$ has area $\frac{\sqrt3}2r^2<\frac{3\sqrt3}4r^2$.

useful_results: For a triangle of circumradius $R$: $\Delta=\frac{abc}{4R}=2R^2\sin A\sin B\sin C$.

Inscribed in a circle of radius $R$: maximum area $\frac{3\sqrt3}4R^2$, maximum perimeter $3\sqrt3\,R$, both for the equilateral triangle; in general the regular $n$-gon has the maximum area $\frac n2R^2\sin\frac{2\pi}n$ (for $n=3$: $1.299R^2$).
Jensen: for concave $\sin$ on $(0,\pi)$, $\sin A+\sin B+\sin C\le3\sin\frac{A+B+C}3=\frac{3\sqrt3}2$; for $\ln\sin$ the product $\sin A\sin B\sin C\le\frac{3\sqrt3}8$.

questions.question: Let $f(x)=\frac{x}{\sqrt{a^2+x^2}}-\frac{d-x}{\sqrt{b^2+(d-x)^2}}$, $x\in\mathbb{R}$, where $a$, $b$ and $d$ are non-zero real constants. Then :
options: $f$ is neither increasing nor decreasing function of $x$
$f'$ is not a continuous function of $x$
questions.key_idea: Each term's derivative is a positive quantity: $\frac{d}{dx}\frac{x}{\sqrt{a^2+x^2}}=\frac{a^2}{(a^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$.
solution: $f'$ is also continuous (a quotient of continuous functions with a non-zero denominator), so (B) is false; $f'>0$ gives (D): $f$ is an increasing function of $x$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Structure: $\frac{t}{\sqrt{c^2+t^2}}=\frac{u}{\sqrt{1+u^2}}$ with $u=\frac t{|c|}$ is an increasing function of $t$, and $f$ is a sum of two such terms.
solution: Write $\frac{x}{\sqrt{a^2+x^2}}=\sin\left(\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{|a|}\right)$: $\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{|a|}$ increases with $x$ on $\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$ and $\sin$ increases there, so this term is increasing.
A sum of increasing functions is increasing, so $f$ is an increasing function of $x$ (D).
(Interpretation: $f$ is the derivative of the path length $L(x)=\sqrt{a^2+x^2}+\sqrt{b^2+(d-x)^2}$, so $f'>0$ says $L$ is convex - the reflection-law problem has a unique minimum.)

useful_results: $\frac{d}{dx}\frac{x}{\sqrt{a^2+x^2}}=\frac{a^2}{(a^2+x^2)^{3/2}}>0$; the function is odd, increasing, bounded in $(-1,1)$ and equals $\sin\left(\tan^{-1}\frac x{|a|}\right)$.

$f(x)=L'(x)$ for $L(x)=\sqrt{a^2+x^2}+\sqrt{b^2+(d-x)^2}$ (shortest broken path / law of reflection); $f'>0$ means $L''>0$, so $L$ is convex with a unique minimum where $f=0$, i.e. $\sin\theta_1=\sin\theta_2$.
A sum of increasing functions is increasing; a function whose derivative is a sum of positive terms needs no sign analysis.

concepts: Rate of change of quantities (related rates)
questions.question: A water tank has the shape of an inverted right circular cone, whose semi-vertical angle is $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac12\right)$. Water is poured into it at a constant rate of 5 cubic metre per minute. Then the rate (in m/min.), at which the level of water is rising at the instant when the depth of water in the tank is 10 m; is :
questions.key_idea: $\tan\theta=\frac rh=\frac12$ gives $h=2r$, so $V$ and $\frac{dV}{dt}$ can be written with $h$ alone.
solution: Given $\frac{dV}{dt}=5\,\text{m}^3/\text{min}$. Let $r$ and $h$ be the radius and depth of the water at any time.

alternate_solutions.idea: Rate of rise $=\frac{\text{rate of filling}}{\text{area of the water surface}}$, since $dV=A\,dh$.
solution: A thin layer of thickness $dh$ at the surface has volume $A\,dh$, where $A$ is the area of the free surface: $\frac{dV}{dt}=A\frac{dh}{dt}$.
At depth $h=10$ the surface radius is $r=h\tan\theta=10\cdot\frac12=5$, so $A=\pi r^2=25\pi$.

useful_results: For any vessel, $\frac{dV}{dt}=A(h)\frac{dh}{dt}$ where $A(h)$ is the area of the free surface at depth $h$.

Cone with semi-vertical angle $\alpha$, apex down: $V=\frac\pi3\tan^2\alpha\,h^3$, so $\frac{dV}{dt}=\pi\tan^2\alpha\,h^2\frac{dh}{dt}$; for $\tan\alpha=\frac12$ this is $\frac{\pi h^2}{4}\frac{dh}{dt}$.
Eliminate extra variables with the fixed ratio ($r=\frac h2$) before differentiating - it avoids a product rule.

questions.question: Let $f:(-1,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined by $f(0)=1$ and $f(x)=\frac1x\log_e(1+x)$, $x\ne0$. Then the function $f$ :
questions.key_idea: $f'(x)$ has the sign of $h(x)=x-(1+x)\ln(1+x)$, and $h$ has its maximum $h(0)=0$.
solution: Sign of $h'$: $+$ on $(-1,0)$ and $-$ on $(0,\infty)$, so $h$ increases up to $x=0$ and decreases after it.
Hence $h$ has its maximum at $x=0$: $h(x)\le h(0)=0$, i.e. $h(x)<0$ for $x\ne0$.
$f$ is continuous at $0$ since $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\ln(1+x)}x=1=f(0)$, so $f$ is decreasing in the whole of $(-1,\infty)$, option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $\frac{\ln(1+x)}{x}=\int_0^1\frac{dt}{1+xt}$; the integrand decreases in $x$ for each $t$, so the integral does too.
solution: So $f(x)=\int_0^1\frac{dt}{1+xt}$ for every $x\in(-1,\infty)$ - including the given value $f(0)=1$.
For each fixed $t\in(0,1]$, $x\mapsto\frac1{1+xt}$ is strictly decreasing on $(-1,\infty)$ (the denominator $1+xt>0$ increases with $x$).
An integral of strictly decreasing functions is strictly decreasing, so $f$ decreases on $(-1,\infty)$: option (A).

useful_results: $\frac{\ln(1+x)}x$ is the slope of the chord of the concave curve $y=\ln(1+x)$ from $(0,0)$, and chord slopes from a fixed point of a concave function decrease; hence $\frac{\ln(1+x)}{x}$ decreases on $(-1,\infty)$ with value $1$ at $0$.
Consequence: $(1+x)\ln(1+x)>x$ for $x>-1$, $x\ne0$ (e.g. $x=1$: $2\ln2=1.386>1$), and $\ln(1+x)\le x$.
$(1+x)^{1/x}=e^{f(x)}$ also decreases on $(-1,\infty)$, tending to $e$ at $0$. Representing a quotient as $\int_0^1$ is a useful monotonicity trick.

questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined as $f(x)=\begin{cases}-55x, & \text{if }x<-5\\ 2x^3-3x^2-120x, & \text{if }-5\le x\le4\\ 2x^3-3x^2-36x-336, & \text{if }x>4,\end{cases}$ Let $A=\{x\in\mathbb{R}:f\text{ is increasing}\}$. Then $A$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Differentiate piece by piece and take, in each piece, the $x$ with $f'>0$; the pieces join continuously.
solution: Intersecting with $(-5,4)$: $x\in(-5,-4)$, so $f$ is increasing there.
Intersecting with $x>4$: $x\in(4,\infty)$, so $f$ is increasing there.
($f$ is continuous at the junctions: $f(-5)=275$ from both sides' formulas, and $f(4)=-400$ from both.) Hence $A=(-5,-4)\cup(4,\infty)$, option (C).
useful_results: For a piecewise function, check continuity at each junction first; then find the sign of $f'$ on each piece and intersect with the piece's interval.
The increasing set is a union of intervals; the answer lists open intervals even though $f$ is also increasing on the closed intervals $[-5,-4]$ and $[4,\infty)$.
$f'$ need not be continuous at junctions: here the one-sided derivatives at $x=4$ are $-48$ and $36$ (a corner that turns decreasing into increasing).

questions.question: For all twice differentiable functions $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, with $f(0)=f(1)=f'(0)=0$,
questions.key_idea: Apply Rolle's theorem to $f$ on $[0,1]$, then to $f'$ between its two zeros $0$ and $\alpha$.
solution: Apply Rolle's theorem to $y=f(x)$ on $[0,1]$: $f(0)=f(1)=0$, so $f'(\alpha)=0$ for some $\alpha\in(0,1)$.
Now apply Rolle's theorem to $y=f'(x)$ on $[0,\alpha]$.
$f'(0)=f'(\alpha)=0$ ($f'$ is continuous and differentiable since $f$ is twice differentiable).
Example $f(x)=x^2(x-1)$: $f''(x)=6x-2$ vanishes only at $x=\frac13$, so it is false that $f''\ne0$ everywhere (B), false that $f''(0)=0$ (C: $f''(0)=-2$) and false that $f''=0$ everywhere (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: If $f''$ never vanishes it has one sign (Darboux), so $f$ is strictly convex or concave; but a strictly convex $f$ with $f'(0)=0$ lies strictly above its tangent $y=0$, contradicting $f(1)=0$.
solution: Suppose $f''(x)\ne0$ for every $x\in(0,1)$. $f''$ is the derivative of $f'$, so by Darboux's theorem it cannot change sign without being $0$: either $f''>0$ throughout $(0,1)$ or $f''<0$ throughout.
If $f''>0$ on $(0,1)$ then $f'$ is strictly increasing on $[0,1]$, so $f'(x)>f'(0)=0$ for $x\in(0,1]$ and $f$ is strictly increasing: $f(1)>f(0)=0$.
This contradicts $f(1)=0$. If $f''<0$, in the same way $f'(x)<0$ for $x>0$, so $f(1)<f(0)=0$ - again a contradiction.

useful_results: Generalised Rolle: if $f$ has $n+1$ zeros counted with multiplicity ($f(0)=f'(0)=0$ is a double zero at $0$, plus $f(1)=0$: three zeros) then $f^{(n)}$ vanishes somewhere inside - here $f''$.
Rolle needs continuity on $[a,b]$ and differentiability on $(a,b)$; applying it to $f'$ needs $f'$ differentiable, which is why 'twice differentiable' is given.
A derivative has the intermediate-value (Darboux) property, so a nowhere-zero derivative has constant sign even if it is not continuous.

concepts: Minimum value of a trigonometric expression
Range of a function using derivatives
questions.question: The minimum value of $\alpha$ for which the equation $\frac4{\sin x}+\frac1{1-\sin x}=\alpha$ has at least one solution in $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: The equation has a solution iff $\alpha$ is in the range of $f(x)=\frac4{\sin x}+\frac1{1-\sin x}$, so $\alpha_{\min}=\min f$ (at $\sin x=\frac23$).
solution: $f(x)=\frac4{\sin x}+\frac1{1-\sin x}=\frac{4-3\sin x}{\sin x(1-\sin x)}$ on $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$, where $0<\sin x<1$.
$f'(x)=\cos x\left[-\frac4{\sin^2x}+\frac1{(1-\sin x)^2}\right]=\frac{\cos x\,(2-\sin x)(3\sin x-2)}{\sin^2x\,(1-\sin x)^2}$.
On $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$, $\cos x>0$ and $2-\sin x>0$, so the sign of $f'$ is the sign of $3\sin x-2$: negative for $\sin x<\frac23$ and positive for $\sin x>\frac23$.
So $f$ has its minimum at $\sin x=\frac23$.
As $\sin x\to0^+$ or $\sin x\to1^-$, $f\to\infty$, so the range of $f$ is $[9,\infty)$ and the equation has a solution iff $\alpha\ge9$. The minimum value of $\alpha$ is $9$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes f'(x) = (2 - sin x)(3 sin x - 2)/(sin^2 x (1 - sin x)^2), omitting the factor cos x that comes from differentiating with respect to x (d/dx of 1/sin x is -cos x / sin^2 x). Since cos x > 0 on (0, pi/2) the sign analysis and the answer 9 are unchanged. The PDF also does not argue that f is unbounded above (so the range is [9, infinity)); added.

solution: Equality needs $\frac2s=\frac1{1-s}$, i.e. $s=\frac23$, which is attainable in $(0,1)$ ($x=\sin^{-1}\frac23\in\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$).
So the minimum value of $\alpha$ is $9$.

useful_results: Titu/Engel form: $\frac{a^2}x+\frac{b^2}{1-x}\ge(a+b)^2$ for $x\in(0,1)$, with equality at $x=\frac{a}{a+b}$; equivalently $\min\left(\frac px+\frac q{1-x}\right)=(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)^2$ (here $p=4,q=1$: $9$ at $x=\frac23$).
Trigonometric version: $\frac{a^2}{\sin^2\theta}+\frac{b^2}{\cos^2\theta}\ge(a+b)^2$, e.g. $\csc^2\theta+\sec^2\theta\ge4$.
'Least $\alpha$ such that $g(x)=\alpha$ has a solution' is $\min g$ when $g$ is continuous and unbounded above; check the behaviour at the ends of the interval.

questions.question: If the tangent to the curve, $y=e^x$ at a point $(c,e^c)$ and the normal to the parabola, $y^2=4x$ at the point $(1,2)$ intersect at the same point on the $x$-axis, then the value of $c$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: Find where the normal to the parabola meets the $x$-axis, then match it with the $x$-intercept $c-1$ of the tangent to $e^x$.
solution: Slope of the tangent $m_T=1$, so slope of the normal $m_N=-1$.
Curve $y=e^x$: $\frac{dy}{dx}=e^x$, so at $(c,e^c)$ the slope is $e^c$.
Both lines meet at the same point of the $x$-axis: $c-1=3$, so $c=4$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Subnormal and subtangent: the parabola's subnormal is the constant $2a=2$ and the subtangent of $e^x$ is the constant $1$.
solution: For $y^2=4ax$ ($a=1$) the subnormal (projection of the normal on the axis) is constant, $=2a=2$. So the normal at $(1,2)$ meets the $x$-axis at $x=1+2=3$.
For $y=e^x$ the subtangent is $\frac{y}{y'}=\frac{e^c}{e^c}=1$, so the tangent at $(c,e^c)$ meets the $x$-axis at $x=c-1$.

useful_results: Parabola $y^2=4ax$: the normal at $(x_1,y_1)$ meets the axis at $x=x_1+2a$ (subnormal $=2a$ always); the tangent meets the axis at $x=-x_1$.
For $y=e^{kx}$ the subtangent is the constant $\frac1k$: the tangent at $x=c$ meets the $x$-axis at $c-\frac1k$.
For tangents/normals meeting on the $x$-axis, equate the $x$-intercepts: set $y=0$ in each line.
